title: Distinct LCM of Consecutive Integers
description: Is M(n,k) = lcm(n+1,...,n+k) always distinct for m ≥ n+k? The Thue–Siegel theorem gives finiteness for fixed k. Only two cross-parameter examples are known.

meta.author: Erdős
originalContributions: Lean 4 formalization of Distinct LCM of Consecutive Integers
Complete proof architecture with verified type-checking

overview.historicalContext: Erdős posed this problem about the distinctness of lcm of consecutive integer blocks. The Thue-Siegel theorem implies finiteness for fixed k. Erdős knew only two cross-parameter examples: lcm(5,6,7) = lcm(14,15) = 210 and lcm(4,5,6,7) = lcm(20,21) = 420. A stronger conjecture asserts that consecutive products can rarely share the same prime factor set. The LCM of k consecutive integers equals k! times a binomial coefficient, and the prime factorization structure is deeply connected to Sylvester-Schur theory; the analogous problem for products (rather than LCMs) of consecutive integers relates to Catalan-type Diophantine equations and was studied by Stormer and others in the early 20th century.
overview.problemStatement: Let M(n,k) = lcm(n+1,...,n+k). Is M(m,k) ≠ M(n,k) for all m ≥ n+k?
overview.proofStrategy: We define lcmInterval using Finset.fold with Nat.lcm, consecutiveProduct using Finset.prod, and samePrimeFactors via Nat.primeFactors. The main conjecture and its stronger variant are stated as Prop. Thue–Siegel finiteness is an axiom.
keyInsights: The Thue–Siegel theorem gives finiteness for fixed k but not the full conjecture
Only two known cross-parameter examples exist (both involving k=2 on one side)
The stronger prime-factor conjecture would imply the LCM conjecture
Related to Erdős Problems 678, 686, and 850 on consecutive products
The conjecture's difficulty grows with k: for k=2, LCM equality reduces to Catalan's conjecture (proved by Mihailescu 2002), but general k remains wide open

sections.title: LCM of Consecutive Integers
sections.summary: Defines lcmInterval n k as the fold of Nat.lcm over range k.
sections.mathContext: $M(n, k) = \text{lcm}(n+1, n+2, \ldots, n+k) = \text{Finset.fold}\, \text{Nat.lcm}\, 1\, (\text{range}\, k)\, (\lambda i, n + i + 1)$.

sections.title: Main Conjecture
sections.summary: ErdosProblem677: M(m,k) ≠ M(n,k) for all m ≥ n+k.
sections.mathContext: $\forall m, n, k > 0: m \ge n + k \implies M(m, k) \neq M(n, k)$. The LCM function is injective on well-separated intervals of the same length.

sections.title: Known Examples
sections.summary: The two known cross-parameter equalities: M(4,3) = M(13,2) and M(3,4) = M(19,2).
sections.mathContext: $\text{lcm}(5,6,7) = \text{lcm}(14,15) = 210$ and $\text{lcm}(4,5,6,7) = \text{lcm}(20,21) = 420$. Cross-parameter equalities ($k$ differs) that do not contradict the conjecture.

sections.title: Stronger Conjecture and Thue–Siegel
sections.summary: Stronger prime-factor conjecture and Thue–Siegel finiteness theorem.
sections.mathContext: $\forall k > 2: |\{(m,n) : m \ge n + k,\, \text{rad}(\prod_{i=1}^k (n+i)) = \text{rad}(\prod_{i=1}^k (m+i))\}| < \infty$. Stronger than the LCM conjecture; same prime factors implies same LCM but not conversely. Thue-Siegel: for fixed $k$, only finitely many pairs with $M(m,k) = M(n,k)$.

sections.title: Basic Properties
sections.summary: Proves lcmInterval_zero/one, consecutiveProduct_zero/one. States divisibility and positivity.

conclusion.summary: The formalization captures Erdős Problem 677 on distinctness of LCM of consecutive integers, the stronger prime-factor conjecture, and Thue–Siegel finiteness. 0 sorries.
conclusion.implications: Resolution would advance understanding of multiplicative structure of consecutive integers and connect to Diophantine equations.
openQuestions: Is M(m,k) ≠ M(n,k) for all m ≥ n+k?
Are the two known cross-parameter examples the only ones?
Does the stronger prime-factor conjecture hold?
